en.title: Banking and Finance: the whole course
en.short: What the Banking and Finance course covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Banking and finance is the study of money, credit and the institutions and markets that move funds from savers to borrowers and investors. Banking looks closely at banks and similar deposit-taking institutions: how they take deposits, lend, manage liquidity and risk, and obey regulation. Finance is wider. It covers corporate finance, investments, financial markets and international finance.

The subject combines economics, accounting, law, statistics and management. It asks how households, firms, banks and governments decide what to save, borrow, lend and invest, often under uncertainty. A bank is not just a shop for money. It transforms maturity and risk, and it depends on public confidence. That is why regulation and ethics belong in the same course as lending and treasury.

These notes are for learning, not professional advice.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities award a BSc in Banking and Finance, usually over four years, under National Universities Commission (NUC) guidance. Polytechnics award ND and HND under National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) guidance, with the HND commonly following the ND. Master’s awards include MSc and MBA. The Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN) offers professional banking qualifications; ask about exemptions directly.

In the United Kingdom, a bachelor’s degree in banking or finance is commonly three years. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years. Master’s degrees are often one or two years. Some programmes include industrial attachment or a dissertation. Professional bodies and universities sometimes grant exemptions from papers, but the rules change, so confirm with the body.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics build the base. You start with the nature and scope of banking and finance, money and the monetary system, and the financial system and institutions. Then come the tools: financial mathematics, business statistics, financial accounting, economics, and business and banking law, including contracts and negotiable instruments. Banking operations and services show how the ideas appear in practice.

Core topics examine the institution and its environment. They include commercial bank management, central banking and monetary policy, bank regulation and supervision, credit analysis and lending, treasury and liquidity management, and risk management. You also study financial markets and instruments, investment analysis and portfolio management, corporate finance, international finance, bank performance analysis, non-bank financial institutions, ethics and corporate governance, financial technology and digital banking, development finance and microfinance, and research methods.

Master’s topics go deeper into theory and evidence: advanced banking theory, financial econometrics, advanced risk management, and advanced bank regulation and financial stability.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the mechanism before the label. For every topic, ask what problem it solves, who bears the risk, and how the bank or market earns its return. In financial mathematics, write the formula, state the units and time period, then check the answer with a rough estimate. In accounting, follow a bank’s balance sheet and income statement until the items make sense.

Use current official sources for regulation and rates. In Nigeria, that means the Central Bank of Nigeria and other regulators; elsewhere, use the central bank and supervisor for that country. Read one bank’s annual report alongside the chapters. Practise short calculations and past questions. Keep a glossary of terms and a one-page map linking each topic to the others.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat banking and finance as the same thing. Banking is about institutions and their risks; finance is about decisions, markets and valuation. Another mistake is memorising definitions without the mechanism, so an answer cannot explain why a bank fails or why a central bank raises a policy rate.

Other frequent errors include:
Ignoring country-specific law and regulation.
Using old rates, fees or capital rules without checking the current source.
Confusing liquidity with capital, or profit with cash flow.
Forgetting units and timing in interest and present value calculations.
Reading only summaries and never attempting full questions.
Not checking the handbook for the award, length and exemptions.

keyPoints: Banking and finance studies how funds move through banks and markets, and how risk is priced and managed.
Banks transform maturity and liquidity, so confidence and regulation are central to the subject.
Awards and course length differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Financial mathematics, accounting, economics and law are the foundation tools of the course.
Regulation and rates are country-specific and change, so use current official sources.
Learn by solving problems and reading real bank reports, not by memorising labels.

en.title: Nature and Scope of Banking and Finance
en.short: Definitions, financial intermediation, roles of savers and borrowers, careers and professional bodies.

sections.heading: Banking and finance defined
sections.text:
Banking is the business of accepting deposits, making loans and providing payment services. Finance is the study of how money is raised, allocated and invested, and the system of institutions and markets that does this. The two overlap: banks are financial institutions, and banking is a major part of finance.

A simple way to see the difference: banking focuses on the operations of deposit-taking institutions, while finance covers a wider field, including corporate investment, asset pricing and personal financial planning.

sections.heading: Financial intermediation
sections.text:
Financial intermediation is the process by which institutions channel funds from savers (surplus units) to borrowers (deficit units). Households save and also borrow for homes and consumption. Firms need capital for investment and working capital. Governments borrow to fund deficits and provide public services. Financial institutions pool small savings, screen borrowers, transform maturities and spread risk.

Case: Amina saves ₦20,000 each month with a microfinance bank in Kano. The bank pools her savings with others and lends to a tailoring business that needs working capital. Amina earns interest; the tailor buys cloth and pays staff. The bank earns a margin between the interest it pays savers and the interest it charges borrowers.

sections.heading: Careers and professional bodies
sections.text: Career paths include retail banking, corporate banking, investment banking, asset management, risk management, compliance, treasury, financial planning and financial technology. Professional bodies and regulators differ by country. In Nigeria, the Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN) offers banking qualifications, and the Central Bank of Nigeria regulates banks. In the UK, the London Institute of Banking & Finance offers qualifications, and the Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority regulate banks. Global bodies include the CFA Institute for investment analysis and GARP for risk management. Always check the current local requirements.

keyPoints: Banking is the business of taking deposits, lending and providing payment services; finance is the wider study and system of raising, allocating and investing money.
Financial intermediation channels funds from surplus units (savers) to deficit units (borrowers).
Households, firms and governments are the main non-financial participants; institutions intermediate between them.
Career paths include retail, corporate and investment banking, asset management, risk, compliance and fintech.
Professional bodies and regulators differ by country; examples include the CIBN in Nigeria and the London Institute of Banking & Finance in the UK.
Always check current local qualification and regulatory requirements.

en.title: Money and the Monetary System
en.short: Functions and evolution of money, legal tender, payments, monetary aggregates and bank money creation.

sections.heading: Functions and forms
sections.text:
Money is anything generally accepted as payment and as a store of value. It acts as a medium of exchange, avoiding barter; a unit of account, pricing goods; a store of value, carrying purchasing power forward; and a standard of deferred payment, allowing debts to be settled later.

Money evolved from commodities such as salt, cowries and metals to coins, notes and bank deposits. Commodity money has value in itself; token money’s value comes from its face value, not its material. Most money today is bank deposits.

sections.heading: Legal tender and payments
sections.text:
Legal tender is money that a country’s law requires creditors to accept for settlement of a debt. The rules are national: Nigeria’s central bank issues naira notes and coins; other countries differ. Legal tender does not always compel a shop to accept a large note for a small purchase, and debts can be settled by agreement in other forms.

Payment systems move money between payers and payees. They include cash, cheques, cards, mobile money and large-value interbank systems. They need rules, participants and a settlement asset, usually central bank money.

sections.heading: Monetary aggregates
sections.text:
Monetary aggregates measure the money stock. M0 or base money usually means currency in circulation plus banks’ reserves at the central bank. M1 usually adds demand deposits to currency. M2 usually adds savings and time deposits.

Definitions differ, so use the central bank’s current table. Aggregates track liquidity but can be distorted by new payment instruments.

sections.heading: Money creation
sections.text:
Commercial banks create deposits when they lend. A loan is recorded as a deposit for the borrower, so new money appears as a bank liability. Banks do not lend out existing deposits one for one; they need reserves, capital and willing borrowers. The central bank sets the price of reserves through policy and may impose reserve requirements.

A simple illustration: with a 10% reserve ratio, the money multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10. If base money is 1,000,000, the simple maximum broad money is 1,000,000 × 10 = 10,000,000. Real systems are less mechanical because cash holdings, capital rules and demand for loans vary. Country rules differ.

keyPoints: Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Legal tender and payment system rules are set nationally, so check the country’s central bank.
Monetary aggregates such as M0, M1 and M2 measure money, but definitions vary by country.
Commercial banks create deposits when they lend, subject to reserves, capital and borrower demand.
Simple money multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio; potential broad money = base money × multiplier.
The simple multiplier overstates real money creation because cash holdings and rules vary.

en.title: The Financial System and Financial Institutions
en.short: Savers, borrowers, intermediaries, markets, instruments and regulators, and how banks differ from non-banks.

sections.heading: What the system does
sections.text: A financial system moves money from people and firms with surplus funds (savers) to those who need funds (borrowers). It also provides payment services and ways to hold wealth. It works through rules and institutions that reduce risk and information gaps. Saving, borrowing, paying and investing are linked parts of one system. The system therefore supports saving, payments and investment.

sections.heading: The six parts
sections.text: Savers supply funds and expect a return. Borrowers demand funds for consumption or investment. Intermediaries, such as banks, stand between them, pooling small deposits and lending larger amounts. Markets are arrangements where claims are bought and sold. Instruments are contracts such as deposits, loans, bonds and shares; each states a claim and a risk. Regulators set and enforce rules, protect users and aim for stability. Example: a bank deposit is an instrument, the bank is an intermediary, and the central bank is a regulator.

sections.heading: Banks and non-banks
sections.text: Banks accept deposits, make loans and run payment systems. Non-bank institutions do some of these without a full banking licence: insurers pool risk, pension funds invest long-term savings, microfinance institutions make small loans, and fintech payment firms move money. They are not commercial banks. Their rules and protections differ by country, so check local law.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Case: Amina saves 20,000 naira monthly in a bank. The bank pools deposits and lends 200,000 naira to Tunde’s bakery for an oven. Tunde repays 220,000 over a year. The extra 20,000 covers interest and risk. Amina earns interest, Tunde invests, and the bank earns a margin. If many savers withdraw at once, the bank may lack cash, which is why regulators set liquidity rules.

keyPoints: A financial system links savers, borrowers, intermediaries, markets, instruments and regulators.
Banks take deposits, lend and operate payments; non-banks provide other financial services under different rules.
Financial intermediaries pool small savings and reduce information and risk problems.
Instruments are contracts such as deposits, loans, bonds and shares.
Regulators set rules and aim to protect users and keep the system stable.
The system supports saving, payments and investment, but liquidity risk remains.

en.title: Financial Mathematics
en.short: Simple and compound interest, present and future value, discounting, annuities and loan schedules.

sections.heading: Interest and compounding
sections.text:
Interest is the price of using money. Principal is the amount borrowed or invested. Simple interest is paid only on principal: I = P × r × t, so FV = P(1 + r t). Compound interest adds interest to principal, so later interest earns interest: FV = PV(1 + r)^n. Here r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods.

Example: P = 100,000 at 10% for 2 years. Simple: FV = 100,000(1 + 0.10 × 2) = 120,000. Compound annually: FV = 100,000(1.10)^2 = 121,000. If 10% is compounded quarterly, r = 0.10 ÷ 4 = 0.025 and n = 4 × 2 = 8, so FV = 100,000(1.025)^8 = 121,840.29. Match r and n to the compounding period.

sections.heading: Present value and discounting
sections.text:
Present value (PV) reverses future value. Discounting finds what a future cash flow is worth now: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. The factor 1 ÷ (1 + r)^n is the discount factor. With m periods per year, use r = i ÷ m and n = m × t, where i is the nominal annual rate and t is years.

Example: 121,000 due in 2 years at 10% annually has PV = 121,000 ÷ (1.10)^2 = 100,000. Tables give factors by n and r; read the row and column.

sections.heading: Annuities and loan schedules
sections.text:
An annuity is a series of equal payments at regular intervals. For an ordinary annuity, payments come at period end. Present value is PV = PMT × [1 − (1 + r)^−n] ÷ r. Future value is FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n − 1) ÷ r].

Loan repayment uses this formula. A loan of 100,000 at 10% for 2 years, repaid annually, has PMT = 100,000 × 0.10 ÷ [1 − (1.10)^−2] = 57,619.05. Year 1: interest 10,000.00, principal 47,619.05, balance 52,380.95. Year 2: interest 5,238.10, principal 52,380.95, balance 0. A schedule lists opening balance, interest, payment, principal and closing balance.

keyPoints: For simple interest, I = P × r × t and FV = P(1 + r t).
Compound interest uses FV = PV(1 + r)^n, where r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods.
Present value is PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n, so discounting reverses compounding.
With m compounding periods per year, use r = i ÷ m and n = m × t.
The present value of an ordinary annuity is PV = PMT × [1 − (1 + r)^−n] ÷ r.
Loan payments use the annuity formula; each payment covers interest first, then principal.

en.title: Business Statistics for Finance
en.short: Descriptive statistics, probability, distributions, sampling, tests, correlation and regression for finance.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a data set. The mean is the arithmetic average. The median is the middle value when data are ordered. The mode is the most frequent value. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean; a large value means returns or profits vary widely. In finance, these measures describe prices, returns, costs and customer balances, and they help compare periods or firms. Check units and whether data are a sample.

sections.heading: Probability and distributions
sections.text: Probability assigns a number from 0 to 1 to an uncertain event. A random variable takes values with probabilities. The binomial distribution counts successes in a fixed number of yes or no trials, such as loan defaults. The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped; many financial returns are modelled with it, though real returns can have fat tails. The expected value is the probability-weighted average outcome.

sections.heading: Sampling and testing
sections.text: A sample is a subset of a population. Random sampling gives every item a known chance of selection and reduces bias. A hypothesis test starts with a null hypothesis, often that a mean or proportion equals a stated value. A test statistic compares the sample estimate with that value. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme if the null is true. If p is below a chosen significance level, often 0.05, reject the null. State the level.

sections.heading: Correlation and regression
sections.text: Correlation r measures the strength of a linear relationship between two variables, from −1 to +1. Simple regression fits y = a + b x, where b is the slope and a the intercept. Example, advertising x and sales y in ₦000: (2,10), (4,14), (6,18). Mean x = 4, mean y = 14. b = Σ[(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)] ÷ Σ(x−x̄)² = 16 ÷ 8 = 2. a = ȳ − b x̄ = 14 − 8 = 6. So y = 6 + 2x: each extra ₦1,000 of advertising is linked to ₦2,000 more sales. Correlation is not proof of cause.

keyPoints: The mean is Σx ÷ n, and the sample standard deviation is √[Σ(x−x̄)² ÷ (n−1)].
Probability lies between 0 and 1, and expected value is Σ(x × P(x)).
The binomial distribution models a fixed number of yes or no trials, while the normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped.
Random sampling reduces bias, and a hypothesis test compares a sample estimate with a null value using a p-value.
Correlation r lies between −1 and +1 and measures linear association, not causation.
In simple regression y = a + b x, b = Σ[(x−x̄)(y−ȳ)] ÷ Σ(x−x̄)² and a = ȳ − b x̄.

en.title: Financial Accounting for Banking
en.short: Double entry, trial balance, the three financial statements and key bank items.

sections.heading: Double-entry bookkeeping
sections.text: Double-entry bookkeeping records every transaction twice: a debit and a credit of equal amount. Debits increase assets and expenses; credits increase liabilities, equity and income. A bank’s loans are assets because customers owe the bank. Customer deposits are liabilities because the bank owes the money back. Interest income is income earned on loans; interest expense is the cost of deposits. For example, a customer deposits 100,000. The bank debits cash 100,000 and credits customer deposits 100,000. If it lends 60,000, it debits loans 60,000 and credits cash 60,000.

sections.heading: Trial balance
sections.text: A trial balance lists every account balance in debit and credit columns at a date. Total debits must equal total credits. It helps find arithmetic errors, but it cannot catch every mistake, such as a transaction posted to the wrong account. Using the example, add interest income accrued 3,000: debit interest receivable 3,000, credit interest income 3,000. Add deposit interest expense 1,000: debit interest expense 1,000, credit interest payable 1,000. Debits: cash 40,000 + loans 60,000 + interest receivable 3,000 + interest expense 1,000 = 104,000. Credits: deposits 100,000 + interest payable 1,000 + interest income 3,000 = 104,000.

sections.heading: The three statements
sections.text: The income statement shows income less expenses for a period. Here interest income 3,000 less interest expense 1,000 gives profit 2,000. The statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at a date: assets = liabilities + equity. Assets are cash 40,000 + loans 60,000 + interest receivable 3,000 = 103,000. Liabilities are deposits 100,000 + interest payable 1,000 = 101,000. Equity is profit 2,000, so 101,000 + 2,000 = 103,000. The statement of cash flows shows cash received and paid, split into operating, investing and financing activities. For a bank, deposits and loans are usually operating, but classification follows the applicable accounting standards.

keyPoints: Every transaction has equal debits and credits.
Total debits must equal total credits in a trial balance.
Profit = income − expenses for the period.
Assets = liabilities + equity at a date.
Loans are bank assets; customer deposits are bank liabilities.
The cash flow statement shows cash movements, not accounting profit.

en.title: Economics for Banking and Finance
en.short: Demand and supply, market structures, output, inflation, unemployment, interest rates and policy.

sections.heading: Demand, supply and markets
sections.text:
Demand is the quantity buyers will take at each price; normally it falls as price rises. Supply is the quantity sellers offer; normally it rises with price. Where the two meet is the equilibrium price. Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to a price change.

Market structure describes competition. Perfect competition has many small firms selling identical goods. A monopoly has one seller. An oligopoly has a few large firms. Monopolistic competition has many firms with differentiated products. Structure shapes pricing power, and so bank margins and lending risk.

sections.heading: Output, inflation, unemployment
sections.text:
National output is measured by gross domestic product (GDP), the value of final goods and services produced in a period. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; it erodes the real value of money. The real interest rate is roughly the nominal rate minus inflation: 14% − 9% = 5%.

Unemployment is the share of the labour force without work but seeking it. Definitions differ by country, so check the official one. Central banks in many countries aim at low, stable inflation and raise interest rates when it rises.

sections.heading: Fiscal and monetary policy
sections.text: Fiscal policy is government taxation and spending. Monetary policy is the central bank’s control of money and interest rates, mainly through its policy rate, the key interest rate it sets to steer the economy. Expansionary policy raises demand; contractionary policy cools it. The two can pull against each other, and their effects reach the economy with a lag.

sections.heading: Why banks care
sections.text:
A bank holds ₦100 million of loans at 12% and ₦80 million of deposits at 5%. Interest income = ₦12m. Interest expense = ₦4m. Net interest income = ₦8m.

If the policy rate rises 2 points and passes through fully (loan and deposit rates rise by the same 2 points): income = ₦14m, expense = ₦5.6m, net = ₦8.4m. Higher rates can widen lending margins, but they also raise default risk, and a slowing economy weakens loan quality.

keyPoints: Equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
Market structure determines pricing power and competitive pressure.
GDP measures national output over a period.
Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation.
Fiscal policy uses tax and spending; monetary policy uses interest rates and money.
Rising rates can widen a bank’s net interest income but also raise credit risk.

en.title: Business and Banking Law: Contracts and Negotiable Instruments
en.short: Contract formation, breach and remedies, agency, bailment, negotiable instruments and loan security.

sections.heading: Forming a contract
sections.text: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement. Common law systems usually require offer, acceptance, consideration (something of value exchanged), intention to create legal relations, capacity and legality. Civil law systems may analyse formation differently. Acceptance must match the offer; a counter-offer rejects it. Some contracts must be in writing, such as certain land or consumer credit agreements, but the list depends on national statute. Check the relevant country’s law.

sections.heading: Breach and remedies
sections.text: Breach occurs when a party fails to perform, performs late or performs badly. Remedies include damages (money compensation), specific performance (a court order to perform) and injunction (an order to stop). Damages aim to put the injured party in the position as if the contract had been performed. Example: Ada agrees to sell Chidi a van for ₦2,000,000, delivery on 1 March. She fails to deliver. Chidi buys a similar van for ₦2,300,000. His basic loss is ₦2,300,000 − ₦2,000,000 = ₦300,000, if he acted reasonably to reduce loss.

sections.heading: Agency and bailment
sections.text: An agent acts for a principal in dealings with third parties. Authority may be actual (express or implied) or apparent (ostensible). The agent owes duties of care, obedience and loyalty, and must account for money. Bailment is delivery of goods by a bailor to a bailee for a purpose, with return or disposal later. The bailee has possession, not ownership, and must take reasonable care. Pawn and bank safe custody are examples. Rules differ by country.

sections.heading: Instruments and security
sections.text: Negotiable instruments are documents representing money that can be transferred by delivery or endorsement (signing the back to transfer it). Types are bills of exchange, cheques and promissory notes. A cheque is a bill drawn on a bank payable on demand. Security for loans includes mortgage (interest in land), charge (right over assets without transfer), pledge (possession of goods), lien (right to retain goods) and guarantee (third party’s promise). Lenders must perfect security (make it enforceable) under national law. Statutes and case law vary, so check national law.

keyPoints: A contract normally needs offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, capacity and legality, but details vary by country.
Breach gives remedies such as damages, specific performance and injunction; damages aim to compensate, subject to foreseeability and the duty to reduce loss.
An agent acts for a principal, and authority may be actual or apparent.
Bailment transfers possession, not ownership, and the bailee must take reasonable care.
Negotiable instruments include bills of exchange, cheques and promissory notes and can be transferred by delivery or endorsement.
Loan security includes mortgage, charge, pledge, lien and guarantee; lenders must perfect it under national law.

en.title: Banking Operations and Services
en.short: Retail and wholesale services, accounts, payments, clearing, channels, due diligence and records.

sections.heading: Retail and wholesale
sections.text: Retail banking serves individuals, households and small businesses. Typical services are current and savings accounts, cards, consumer loans and everyday payments. Wholesale banking serves large companies, institutions and government. It handles high-value payments, trade finance, custody and treasury services. A bank may do both, but the risks, amounts and customer checks differ. Service quality matters in both: customers judge reliability, speed, staff knowledge and how complaints are handled.

sections.heading: Accounts and payments
sections.text: A current or checking account is for frequent transactions and usually pays little or no interest. A savings account holds deposits and pays interest. A fixed or time deposit locks money for an agreed term, often at a higher rate. Payments include cash, cheques, cards, credit transfers, direct debits and mobile money. Each payment carries an instruction: who pays, who receives, how much and when. Banks must verify mandates (the signed instructions on who may operate an account and how) and available funds before debiting an account.

sections.heading: Clearing and settlement
sections.text: Clearing is the process of exchanging, checking and reconciling payment instructions between banks. Settlement is the actual transfer of funds that discharges the payment. Settlement may use accounts at a central bank or a designated payment system. Finality means the payment cannot be reversed. Channels include branches, ATMs, point-of-sale terminals, internet and mobile banking, and agent banking. Digital channels are faster and cheaper but raise fraud and outage risks.

sections.heading: Due diligence and records
sections.text: Customer due diligence (CDD) means identifying a customer, verifying identity, understanding the purpose of the account and monitoring activity. Know your customer (KYC) is part of this. Enhanced checks apply to higher-risk customers. Banks keep account opening forms, identity documents, mandates, transaction records, reconciliations, complaints and audit trails. Retention periods differ by country, so check local law. Example: Amina in Kano deposits cash at a branch. The bank records it, then sends her transfer to a supplier at another bank through clearing; settlement moves the funds.

keyPoints: Retail banking serves individuals and small businesses; wholesale banking serves large corporates, institutions and government.
Clearing checks and reconciles payment instructions; settlement transfers funds and gives finality.
Current accounts support transactions, savings accounts earn interest, and fixed deposits lock funds for a term.
Customer due diligence identifies and verifies customers and monitors their activity.
Service quality depends on reliability, speed, staff knowledge and complaint handling.
Banks must keep accurate operational records, with retention periods set by national law.

en.title: Commercial Bank Management
en.short: Banks earn spreads, manage balance sheets and price products while balancing growth, risk and liquidity.

sections.heading: Business model
sections.text:
A commercial bank takes deposits and other funds, lends and invests them, and earns a spread: the interest it earns on assets is more than the interest it pays on funds. Fees add income, and profit is what remains after operating costs. Its model depends on confidence, reach, credit skill and liquidity. Banks also earn fees from payments, cards and accounts.

Profit is not the only goal. Managers must hold enough capital and liquid assets to absorb losses and meet withdrawals.

sections.heading: Balance sheet and ALM
sections.text:
The balance sheet lists assets (uses of funds) such as loans, cash and securities, and liabilities (sources of funds) such as deposits, borrowings and bonds. Equity is the owners’ stake.

Asset-liability management (ALM) coordinates the mix and maturities of assets and liabilities so interest-rate and liquidity risks stay acceptable. Funding long loans with short deposits creates refinancing risk. ALM sets limits and plans for gaps, the mismatches between asset and liability maturities.

sections.heading: Pricing and channels
sections.text:
Product pricing must cover funding cost, expected credit loss, operating cost, a capital charge (the return required on the capital tied up) and a margin. A loan rate below true cost destroys value even if volume grows.

Channel management decides how customers reach the bank: branches, agents, ATMs, mobile apps and partners. Digital channels cut cost per transaction but need security and reliable service. Channels affect cross-selling and retention.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Illustrative example: earning assets are 1,000 million and the funding rate is 4%. The asset yield is 9%. Net interest income = (9% − 4%) × 1,000 = 50 million before costs and losses. Operating cost is 20 million and expected loss is 10 million, so profit before tax = 20 million. With equity of 100 million, return on equity (before tax) = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.

Growth by lending more raises profit but uses liquidity and capital. Managers trade growth against risk and liquidity.

keyPoints: A bank earns a spread between asset yields and funding costs, plus fees.
Assets are uses of funds; liabilities and equity are sources of funds.
ALM matches maturities and limits interest-rate and liquidity risk.
Loan pricing must cover funding, expected loss, operating cost, capital and margin.
Net interest income = (asset yield − funding rate) × earning assets.
Return on equity = profit ÷ equity; growth must be balanced against risk and liquidity.

en.title: Central Banking and Monetary Policy
en.short: Central bank functions, monetary policy tools, transmission, independence and effects on inflation and output.

sections.heading: Functions and mandate
sections.text: A central bank manages a country’s money and banking system. It issues currency, acts as banker to government and commercial banks, runs payment systems, holds reserves, and lends in a crisis as lender of last resort. It conducts monetary policy: actions to influence money, credit and interest rates. Mandates differ. The European Central Bank’s primary objective is price stability. The US Federal Reserve has a dual mandate of price stability and maximum employment. In a currency union such as the West African Economic and Monetary Union, the regional central bank sets policy for members.

sections.heading: Instruments and transmission
sections.text: Main instruments are the policy rate, open market operations (buying or selling securities to add or drain reserves), reserve requirements and standing facilities (overnight lending and deposit windows at the central bank). Some use quantitative easing, large-scale asset purchases when rates are near zero. Transmission works through several channels. A higher policy rate raises money-market rates, then bank lending and deposit rates. It also affects asset prices, the exchange rate and expectations. Higher borrowing costs reduce consumption and investment, cooling demand and inflation. Output may fall in the short run. Check: if the policy rate is 12% and inflation is 9%, the real policy rate is 12 − 9 = 3%. If inflation falls to 6% while the rate stays 12%, the real rate rises to 6%, so policy tightens without a nominal change.

sections.heading: Independence and accountability
sections.text: Central bank independence means freedom from short-term political pressure in setting policy. Instrument independence is the power to choose tools; goal independence is the power to set the target. Most combine independence with accountability: published decisions, minutes, reports to parliament and inflation targets set by government, as in the United Kingdom. Independence helps credibility but does not remove the need to coordinate with fiscal policy. Financial stability is another duty: central banks watch credit growth, asset bubbles and bank liquidity, using macroprudential tools such as capital buffers. Arrangements vary by country, so check the central bank act and current mandate.

keyPoints: Central banks issue currency, act as banker and lender of last resort, and conduct monetary policy.
Core instruments include the policy rate, open market operations, reserve requirements and standing facilities.
Transmission runs from policy rates to market rates, credit, asset prices, exchange rates and expectations.
Real policy rate = nominal policy rate − inflation.
Independence needs accountability through published decisions, reports and targets.
Financial stability duties use macroprudential tools and vary by country.

en.title: Bank Regulation and Supervision
en.short: Why banks are regulated, licensed, capital and liquidity rules, supervision, deposit cover and AML.

sections.heading: Why regulate banks
sections.text: Banks hold deposits repayable on demand and lend for long terms. A run can force asset sales and spread panic, so regulation protects depositors and the payment system. It also limits systemic risk, the danger that one failure harms many others. Regulation sets rules; supervision checks that banks follow them.

sections.heading: Licensing and prudential rules
sections.text: Licensing means a bank needs the regulator’s permission to operate, with fit owners and managers. Prudential rules concern safety: capital and liquidity. Capital absorbs losses. Risk-weighted assets (RWA) are loans and other exposures weighted by risk. The capital ratio is capital divided by RWA. Liquidity rules require enough cash and safe assets to meet outflows. Basel Committee standards guide many countries, but national rules differ and change, so check the current regulator.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Made-up figures, currency units omitted. RWA = 800. Common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital = 80. CET1 ratio = 80 divided by 800 = 10%. Total capital = 100, so total capital ratio = 100 divided by 800 = 12.5%. High-quality liquid assets = 150; expected net outflows over 30 days = 100. Liquidity coverage ratio = 150 divided by 100 = 150%. A ratio above the local minimum is not proof of safety; asset quality and funding stability also matter.

sections.heading: Supervision, deposit protection, AML
sections.text: Supervisors inspect books, test risks and can restrict business or remove managers. Deposit insurance repays depositors up to a limit if a bank fails; schemes and limits vary by country. Anti-money-laundering (AML) rules require customer due diligence, often called know your customer (KYC), record keeping and reporting of suspicious transactions to the financial intelligence unit. Compliance is checked by supervisors and can lead to fines.

keyPoints: Regulation sets rules; supervision checks that banks follow them.
Capital ratio = capital divided by risk-weighted assets.
Liquidity coverage ratio = high-quality liquid assets divided by net cash outflows over 30 days.
Basel Committee standards are not law; each country adopts its own rules.
Deposit insurance schemes and limits vary by country.
AML requires KYC and reports of suspicious transactions.

en.title: Credit Analysis and Lending
en.short: Assessing borrowers, structuring and pricing loans, collateral, covenants, monitoring and managing bad loans.

sections.heading: Lending and creditworthiness
sections.text: The lending process runs from application and appraisal to approval, documentation, disbursement, monitoring and repayment. Appraisal asks whether the borrower can repay from cash flow, not just security. Lenders often use the 5 Cs: character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. Capacity is central: analyse cash flow and compute the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), which is cash available for debt service divided by debt service. A DSCR below 1 means the cash flow cannot cover payments.

sections.heading: Structuring and pricing
sections.text: Structuring sets amount, tenor (loan duration), repayment schedule, rate and fees. Pricing should cover cost of funds, operating costs, expected loss and profit. Expected loss = probability of default (PD) × loss given default (LGD) × exposure at default (EAD). Collateral is security the lender can sell on default; it lowers LGD but does not replace cash flow. Covenants are contractual promises, such as keeping gearing below a limit or supplying accounts. They give the lender early control.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up firm borrows $500,000. PD is 2% and LGD is 45%. Expected loss = 0.02 × 0.45 × 500,000 = $4,500. Cash available for debt service is $120,000 and debt service is $100,000. DSCR = 120,000 ÷ 100,000 = 1.2, a 20% cushion. If cost of funds is 6%, operating cost 2%, expected loss 0.9% (4,500 ÷ 500,000) and profit margin 1.5%, an indicative rate is 6 + 2 + 0.9 + 1.5 = 10.4%. These figures are illustrative.

sections.heading: Monitoring and workout
sections.text: After disbursement, monitor repayment, account conduct, sales and covenant compliance. Early warning signs include late payments, frequent overdraft use, falling margins and missed reporting. A non-performing loan (NPL) is commonly one overdue by more than 90 days, though definitions vary. Provisioning sets aside an expense for expected credit losses; IFRS 9 requires expected credit loss accounting in many countries. Workout means resolving a troubled loan. Options include restructuring, temporary payment relief, legal action, selling collateral or write-off. Choose by comparing recovery value with cost and delay.

keyPoints: The 5 Cs of credit are character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions.
DSCR = cash available for debt service ÷ debt service; a DSCR below 1 means cash flow cannot cover payments.
Expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD.
Loan pricing should cover the cost of funds, operating costs, expected loss and a profit margin.
Collateral lowers loss given default but does not replace cash flow.
Monitor for early warning signs; an NPL is commonly a loan overdue by more than 90 days, and provisioning rules vary by country and accounting standard.

en.title: Bank treasury and liquidity management
en.short: Treasury, reserves, liquidity gaps, money market funding, repricing risk and liquidity-profitability trade-off.
keywords: interest rate risk in banking book

sections.heading: Treasury and reserves
sections.text: Treasury is the unit that manages the bank’s cash, funding, liquidity and market risk. It keeps reserves: cash and balances at the central bank. Required reserves are set by the central bank and vary by country; excess reserves are a buffer. Liquidity means holding enough cash or assets that can be sold quickly to meet outflows without a fire sale. Money market operations are short-term borrowing and lending, often through repos (sale and repurchase agreements), Treasury bills and interbank deposits. A funding plan sets the mix and maturities of deposits, wholesale borrowing and capital.

sections.heading: Liquidity gaps
sections.text: A liquidity gap compares inflows and outflows in a time bucket. Gap = inflows − outflows. A negative gap is a shortfall to fund. Cumulative gaps show pressure over several buckets. Treasury covers gaps with liquid buffers, interbank borrowing or central bank facilities.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up bank has one-month inflows of ₦120 million and outflows of ₦150 million. Liquidity gap = 120 − 150 = −₦30 million. It must borrow ₦30 million or use its buffer. Its rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, which reprice within the period, are ₦500 million and ₦450 million. Repricing gap = 500 − 450 = +₦50 million. If rates rise by 1 percentage point (0.01), change in net interest income ≈ ₦50 million × 0.01 = ₦0.5 million. A fall in rates would reduce income by the same amount. This is interest rate risk in the banking book: mismatched repricing of assets and liabilities.

sections.heading: Funding and trade-off
sections.text: Funding plans diversify sources and match maturities to reduce rollover risk (the risk that funds cannot be renewed). Liquid assets earn little; loans earn more but are illiquid. Holding more liquidity lowers profitability but reduces the chance of a costly cash shortfall. Treasury balances this trade-off within the board’s risk limits and the regulator’s liquidity rules. Basel III sets international liquidity standards, such as the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) and net stable funding ratio (NSFR), applied through national rules.

keyPoints: Treasury manages cash, funding, liquidity and market risk, and holds required reserves set by the central bank plus an excess buffer.
Liquidity gap = inflows − outflows in a time bucket; a negative gap must be funded.
Repricing gap = rate-sensitive assets − rate-sensitive liabilities; ΔNII ≈ gap × Δr.
Interest rate risk in the banking book comes from mismatched repricing of assets and liabilities.
Liquid assets protect against shortfalls but earn less, so liquidity and profitability trade off.
Funding plans should diversify sources and match maturities; Basel III LCR and NSFR are applied by national regulators.

en.title: Risk Management in Banking
en.short: The main banking risks, risk appetite, controls, stress testing and expected credit loss.

sections.heading: Main banking risks
sections.text: Credit risk is the loss if a borrower or counterparty fails to pay. Market risk is loss from moves in prices, interest rates or exchange rates. Operational risk is loss from failed internal processes, people, systems or external events. Liquidity risk is being unable to meet cash needs without unacceptable cost. Reputational risk is loss of trust among customers, investors and regulators. These risks interact: a credit shock can drain liquidity and damage reputation.

sections.heading: Risk appetite and framework
sections.text: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk a bank is willing to accept to meet its goals. It is set by the board and expressed in limits. Identification asks what could go wrong. Measurement uses models and data, such as probability of default for credit or value at risk for market risk, a loss threshold for a set confidence level and period. Controls include policies, approval limits, segregation of duties and collateral. Stress testing asks how the bank would cope if conditions worsen sharply. Risk reporting gives management and the board regular, clear information. All of this sits in an enterprise risk framework that treats risks together, not in separate silos.

sections.heading: Worked example: expected loss
sections.text: Worked example: expected credit loss. Expected loss (EL) = probability of default (PD) × loss given default (LGD) × exposure at default (EAD). LGD is the share of the exposure lost if default occurs. A bank has a loan exposure of 10,000,000 naira, PD of 2% and LGD of 45%. EL = 0.02 × 0.45 × 10,000,000 = 90,000 naira. In a stress test, PD rises to 5%. Stressed EL = 0.05 × 0.45 × 10,000,000 = 225,000 naira. The bank compares this with its capital and limits. The example is illustrative; real banks estimate PD and LGD from data and regulation.

keyPoints: Credit risk is default loss; market risk is price, rate or exchange rate loss; operational risk is process, people, system or event loss; liquidity risk is inability to meet cash needs; reputational risk is lost trust.
Risk appetite is the risk a bank accepts, set by the board and expressed in limits.
Expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD, where PD is probability of default, LGD is loss given default and EAD is exposure at default.
Stress testing checks whether the bank can survive worse conditions.
An enterprise risk framework identifies, measures, controls, tests and reports risks together.
Risk reporting must reach management and the board regularly and clearly.

en.title: Financial Markets and Instruments
en.short: Money and capital markets, primary and secondary trading, bonds, equities, derivatives, yields and regulation.

sections.heading: Market types
sections.text:
Money markets trade short-term claims, maturing within one year: treasury bills, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. Capital markets trade long-term claims, mainly bonds and equities. The primary market is where an issuer sells new securities to raise funds. The secondary market is where investors later trade existing securities; it provides liquidity and price discovery.

Participants include issuers, investors and intermediaries such as brokers and dealers. Trading is on organised exchanges or over the counter (OTC), a decentralised dealer market. Settlement transfers cash against securities, through a clearing house that reduces counterparty risk.

sections.heading: Bonds and equities
sections.text:
A bond is a loan to an issuer. It pays a coupon, usually fixed, and repays principal at maturity. Its price moves inversely to market yields. Current yield = annual coupon ÷ price. Yield to maturity (YTM) is the single discount rate that makes the present value of future cash flows equal the price.

An equity share is part ownership. The holder receives dividends if declared and gains or loses from price changes. Dividend yield = annual dividend per share ÷ price.

Worked example: a one-year bond has face value 1,000, coupon 10%, and market yield 12%. Cash flow = 1,000 + 100 = 1,100. Price = 1,100 ÷ 1.12 = 982.14. Current yield = 100 ÷ 982.14 = 10.18%, below the 12% YTM because the bond is bought below par.

sections.heading: Derivatives and regulation
sections.text:
A derivative is a contract whose value depends on an underlying asset, rate or price. Main types are forwards (customised future trade), futures (standardised, exchange-traded), options (a right, not an obligation, to buy or sell) and swaps (exchange of cash flows). They can hedge risk or speculate, and can magnify losses.

Market regulation aims to protect investors, ensure fair and orderly trading, require disclosure, and deter manipulation and fraud. Regulators license intermediaries and supervise exchanges and clearing houses. Rules and regulators differ by country; for example, Nigeria and Ghana each have a Securities and Exchange Commission.

keyPoints: Money market instruments mature within one year; capital market instruments are longer term.
The primary market raises new funds; the secondary market provides liquidity and price discovery.
Bond prices move inversely to market yields; current yield = annual coupon ÷ price.
For a one-year bond, price = (coupon + face value) ÷ (1 + market yield).
Equity holders own part of the firm and receive dividends only if declared.
Derivatives transfer risk but can magnify losses, so market regulation requires disclosure and fair trading.

en.title: Investment Analysis and Portfolio Management
en.short: Risk and return, valuation, diversification, CAPM, portfolio construction and performance limits.

sections.heading: Risk and return
sections.text: Return is the gain or loss from an investment, usually a percentage of the amount invested. Expected return is a probability-weighted average of possible returns. Risk is the chance that actual return differs from expected return, often measured by standard deviation. Risk-averse investors demand higher expected return for more risk. A security’s value is the present value of its expected future cash flows, discounted at the required return.

sections.heading: Diversification and CAPM
sections.text:
Diversification means holding assets whose returns do not move together. It reduces unsystematic risk, the risk specific to a firm or industry, because losses in one holding may be offset by gains in another. Systematic risk, the risk of the whole market, remains. Beta measures sensitivity to market movements. The capital asset pricing model (CAPM) gives required return: E(Ri) = Rf + βi × [E(Rm) − Rf], where Rf is the risk-free rate and E(Rm) is the expected return on the market.

Example: Rf = 5%, E(Rm) = 11%, β = 1.2.
E(Ri) = 5% + 1.2 × 6% = 12.2%.

sections.heading: Valuation and portfolios
sections.text:
A share pays a dividend of 2.00 next year. Dividends grow 4% a year and the required return is 12%.
P0 = D1 ÷ (r − g) = 2.00 ÷ 0.08 = 25.00.

Portfolio construction combines assets to reach a target return for acceptable risk, often by mixing a risk-free asset with a diversified portfolio. Weights, correlations and the investor’s risk tolerance guide the choice.

sections.heading: Performance and limits
sections.text:
Performance evaluation compares realised return with risk taken. The Sharpe ratio is (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp, where σp is the portfolio’s standard deviation.

Example: Rp = 14%, Rf = 5%, σp = 18%.
Sharpe = 9 ÷ 18 = 0.50.

Models have limits: CAPM assumptions are unrealistic, betas change, and markets show frictions, taxes and irrational behaviour. Use several measures, not one.

keyPoints: Expected return is a probability-weighted average of possible returns.
Diversification reduces unsystematic risk but not systematic risk.
CAPM: E(Ri) = Rf + βi × [E(Rm) − Rf].
Dividend growth model: P0 = D1 ÷ (r − g).
Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf) ÷ σp.
Model outputs are estimates, so use several measures.

en.title: Corporate Finance
en.short: NPV appraisal, cost of capital, capital structure, dividend policy and working capital.

sections.heading: Investment appraisal
sections.text:
Net present value (NPV) discounts expected cash flows at the cost of capital and subtracts the initial outlay: NPV = Σ CF_t ÷ (1+r)^t − outlay. A positive NPV adds value, so accept the project. The internal rate of return (IRR) makes NPV zero; it is useful but can mislead when cash flows change sign. Payback ignores the time value of money.

Example: a machine costs ₦1,000,000 and returns ₦600,000 at the end of each of two years. At r = 10%, NPV = 600,000 ÷ 1.10 + 600,000 ÷ 1.21 − 1,000,000 = 545,455 + 495,868 − 1,000,000 = ₦41,323. Accept it.

sections.heading: Cost of capital
sections.text: The cost of capital is the minimum return investors require. Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) mixes the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt: WACC = (E ÷ V) × r_e + (D ÷ V) × r_d × (1 − T), where V = E + D and T is the tax rate. Use WACC only for projects with similar risk; a riskier project needs a higher rate.

sections.heading: Capital and dividends
sections.text: Capital structure is the mix of debt and equity. Modigliani and Miller showed that, in perfect markets without taxes, this mix does not change firm value. With taxes, interest is tax-deductible, so debt can add value, but higher debt raises financial risk and distress costs. Dividend policy sets how much profit is paid out. In perfect markets it does not affect value; in practice taxes, signalling and investor preferences can matter.

sections.heading: Working capital
sections.text: Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Managers balance cash, inventory, receivables and payables. The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days; a shorter cycle frees cash. Financing choices affect value and risk: more debt raises fixed payments and can lift return on equity in good years, but it also raises the chance of financial distress.

keyPoints: NPV = Σ CF_t ÷ (1+r)^t − initial outlay; accept projects with positive NPV.
IRR is the rate where NPV = 0, but it can mislead when cash flows change sign.
WACC = (E ÷ V) × r_e + (D ÷ V) × r_d × (1 − T) is the minimum return for projects of similar risk.
In perfect markets without taxes, capital structure and dividend policy do not change firm value; taxes and distress costs can make debt matter.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities, and the cash conversion cycle = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.
More debt raises fixed payments and financial risk, so financing choices affect both expected return and the chance of distress.

en.title: International Finance
en.short: Foreign exchange, exchange rates, balance of payments, trade finance and currency hedging.

sections.heading: Markets and quotations
sections.text:
The foreign exchange market is where currencies are traded. Most deals are over the counter. Spot deals settle quickly; forward deals settle later. A quotation has a base and a quote currency. In USD/NGN the base is the US dollar and the quote is the naira, so the rate is naira per dollar. Direct quotation gives local currency per foreign unit; indirect gives the reverse. Rates are determined by supply and demand, expectations, interest rates and prices. Purchasing power parity compares price levels; interest rate parity links spot and forward rates. Central banks may intervene. Conventions differ by country.

The market is decentralised, so no single price applies everywhere at once.

sections.heading: Balance of payments
sections.text:
The balance of payments records a country’s transactions with the rest of the world. The current account covers goods, services, income and transfers. The capital and financial accounts cover investment and loans. Errors and omissions balance the accounts, and reserves change. A current account deficit must be financed by inflows or reserves. Definitions follow the IMF manual, but data quality varies.

A surplus in one account is matched by a deficit or lending elsewhere. The accounts must balance in total, not each part separately.

sections.heading: Regimes and trade finance
sections.text: Exchange rate regimes range from hard pegs such as currency boards to floating rates, with managed floats in between. The choice affects policy and risk, and legal rules differ by country. Trade finance supports imports and exports. A letter of credit makes a bank promise to pay against documents. Bills of exchange, documentary collections and guarantees also reduce payment risk. Terms follow ICC rules such as UCP 600, but local law still applies.

sections.heading: Currency risk and hedging
sections.text: Currency risk has three forms: transaction risk on future payments, translation risk on reporting foreign assets, and economic risk on competitiveness. Hedging uses forwards, futures, options, swaps or natural offsets. Example: a Nigerian importer owes $100,000 in 90 days. The spot rate is ₦1,500/$ and the forward rate is ₦1,560/$, illustrative. A forward contract costs 100,000 × 1,560 = ₦156,000,000. If the naira falls to ₦1,650/$, the spot cost would be ₦165,000,000, so the forward saves ₦9,000,000. Hedging removes uncertainty but may forgo a gain.

keyPoints: In USD/NGN the base is the US dollar and the quote is the naira, so the rate is naira per dollar.
Exchange rates respond to supply and demand, interest rates, prices and expectations, and central banks may intervene.
The balance of payments records current, capital and financial transactions and must balance in total.
Fixed, floating and managed regimes create different policy choices, and rules differ by country.
Forward cost = foreign currency amount × forward rate.
Hedging result = foreign amount × (future spot rate − forward rate); a positive result is the saving.

en.title: Bank Performance Analysis
en.short: How to read bank statements and compute profitability, asset quality, capital and liquidity ratios.

sections.heading: Reading bank statements
sections.text: A bank’s annual report contains the income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement and notes. Read the notes and regulatory disclosures: they explain accounting policies, loan classifications, provisions, capital and liquidity. Bank statements differ from those of a manufacturer because loans are the main assets and deposits are the main funding. Profit is interest income less interest expense, plus fees, less operating costs and loan losses. Use average balances where possible, because year-end figures may be unusual.

sections.heading: Four ratio families
sections.text: Profitability: ROA = net profit ÷ average total assets; ROE = net profit ÷ average equity; net interest margin = net interest income ÷ average earning assets; cost-to-income = operating expenses ÷ operating income. Asset quality: NPL ratio = non-performing loans ÷ gross loans; coverage = loan loss allowance ÷ NPLs. Capital adequacy ratio = regulatory capital ÷ risk-weighted assets. Liquidity: liquid assets ÷ total assets; loan-to-deposit ratio = net loans ÷ deposits. Definitions vary, so compare like with like.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up bank reports, in millions of naira: net profit 120; average assets 4,000; average equity 500; operating expenses 240; operating income 480; gross loans 2,500; NPLs 125; allowance 75; regulatory capital 480; risk-weighted assets 3,200; liquid assets 600; deposits 3,000; net loans 2,400. ROA = 120 ÷ 4,000 = 3%. ROE = 120 ÷ 500 = 24%. Cost-to-income = 240 ÷ 480 = 50%. NPL ratio = 125 ÷ 2,500 = 5%. Coverage = 75 ÷ 125 = 60%. Capital adequacy = 480 ÷ 3,200 = 15%. Liquid assets ratio = 600 ÷ 4,000 = 15%. Loan-to-deposit = 2,400 ÷ 3,000 = 80%.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and limits
sections.text: Benchmarking compares ratios with the bank’s past years, peers and regulatory minima. Trend analysis asks why a ratio moved. Comparisons across banks and countries are limited by different accounting rules, loan definitions, tax, inflation, regulation and business models. A high ROE may come from high leverage or risk. Read ratios together, not alone.

keyPoints: ROA = net profit ÷ average total assets; ROE = net profit ÷ average equity.
NPL ratio = non-performing loans ÷ gross loans; coverage = loan loss allowance ÷ NPLs.
Capital adequacy ratio = regulatory capital ÷ risk-weighted assets.
Liquidity ratios include liquid assets ÷ total assets and net loans ÷ deposits.
Compare ratios over time, with peers and against regulatory minima, using consistent definitions.
Cross-country comparisons are limited by accounting, regulation, tax, inflation and business model differences.

en.title: Non-Bank Financial Institutions
en.short: Insurance, pensions, leasing, finance houses and CIS: roles, risks, regulation and links with banks.

sections.heading: The main types
sections.text: Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) are licensed financial firms that are not commercial banks. Insurance companies pool premiums from many policyholders and pay claims; they transfer risk. Pension funds collect contributions and invest them to pay retirement benefits. Leasing firms own an asset and let a business use it for a rental; the lessee may buy it at the end. Finance houses lend, often for consumer goods or business equipment, and may take deposits only if licensed. Collective investment schemes (CIS) pool money from many investors and buy a portfolio under a fund manager.

sections.heading: Roles and risks
sections.text: NBFIs fill gaps banks cannot. Insurers make risks manageable. Pension funds provide long-term investment. Leasing lets a firm use equipment without buying it. Finance houses serve borrowers banks may reject. CIS give savers diversification, which means spreading money across assets. Risks differ: insurers face claims and investment risk; pension funds face longevity risk (members living longer than expected) and investment risk; leasing firms face credit and resale value risk; finance houses face credit and funding risk; CIS face market, liquidity and mis-selling risk.

sections.heading: Regulation and banks
sections.text: Regulation varies by country. It covers licensing, capital, conduct and disclosure. In Nigeria, insurance is regulated by NAICOM, pensions by PenCom, securities and CIS by SEC, and finance houses by the Central Bank of Nigeria. Banks and NBFIs compete for savings and customers, but they cooperate. Where allowed, banks may distribute insurance as bancassurance, meaning selling insurance through banks, hold pension fund assets, lend to finance houses, or sell CIS. NBFIs provide services banks lack. Depositors in banks may have deposit insurance; NBFI customers usually do not, so check the local scheme.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Ada runs a Lagos printing business. A leasing firm buys a ₦2,000,000 printer and leases it to her for 24 months. She avoids a cash payment, while the lessor keeps ownership until the final payment. If Ada defaults, the lessor can repossess it, but its resale value may fall. The lessor checks her cash flow and sets a deposit.

keyPoints: NBFIs are licensed financial firms other than commercial banks.
Insurers transfer risk, pension funds provide long-term savings, leasing supplies asset use, finance houses lend, and collective investment schemes pool investments.
Each type carries distinct risks, including claims, longevity, credit, resale value, market and mis-selling risk.
Regulation usually covers licensing, capital, conduct and disclosure, and it varies by country.
Banks and NBFIs compete for customers but cooperate through bancassurance, holding pension assets, lending and distribution.
Deposit insurance for banks does not normally cover NBFI products, so customers should check the local scheme.

en.title: Ethics and Corporate Governance in Banking
en.short: Fiduciary duty, conflicts, insider dealing, whistleblowing, board oversight, disclosure and risk governance.

sections.heading: Duty and conflicts
sections.text: A fiduciary duty is a legal duty to act in another person’s best interest. Bank directors owe duties of loyalty and care to the company; staff who handle client money or give advice may owe fiduciary duties to clients. A conflict of interest arises when personal interest, or another role, could sway that duty. Firms must identify, disclose and manage conflicts, for example by separating deal teams from sales teams. A made-up case: at Adeyemi Bank, a loan officer sits on a customer’s tender panel and owns shares in a bidder. She should declare the interest and step aside.

sections.heading: Insider dealing and abuse
sections.text: Insider dealing is trading, or tipping others to trade, on price-sensitive information not yet public. Market abuse is wider: it includes insider dealing, market manipulation and false or misleading statements that distort prices. Rules and penalties differ by country, so check the local securities law and regulator. Controls include restricted lists of securities staff may not trade, clear dealing rules for staff and surveillance of trades. For example, if a bank employee bought shares before a takeover announcement, that would be insider dealing; the bank must report it to the regulator.

sections.heading: Whistleblowing and codes
sections.text: Whistleblowing is reporting wrongdoing inside or outside an organisation. Good systems offer confidential channels, protect reporters from retaliation and require independent follow-up; legal protection varies by country. Professional codes set ethical standards for bankers, such as honesty, competence and confidentiality. They guide behaviour but do not replace law or a firm’s own rules.

sections.heading: Board and risk governance
sections.text: The board sets strategy, appoints senior management and approves risk appetite, the level of risk it is willing to accept. Disclosure means giving shareholders and regulators timely, accurate information. Internal control uses policies, segregation of duties, reconciliations and independent audit to safeguard assets and produce reliable reports. Risk governance assigns clear responsibility: a board risk committee, a chief risk officer and three lines of defence, where business units own risk, risk functions oversee it and internal audit gives independent assurance.

keyPoints: Fiduciary duty requires acting in another person’s best interest and managing conflicts.
Insider dealing and market abuse undermine fair markets and are controlled by law and firm rules.
Whistleblowing channels protect reporters and help detect misconduct.
Professional codes set ethical standards but do not replace legal rules.
The board sets strategy and risk appetite and oversees disclosure, while internal control safeguards assets.
Risk governance needs clear roles such as a board risk committee, a chief risk officer and three lines of defence.

en.title: Financial Technology and Digital Banking
en.short: Digital payments, mobile money, core and open banking, cryptoassets, robo-advisory, risks and regulation.

sections.heading: Payments and mobile money
sections.text: Digital payment is the electronic transfer of money between accounts or devices. Mobile money stores value in an account linked to a phone, with cash paid in and out through agents, often for people without bank accounts. M-Pesa in Kenya is a well-known example. A trader can receive payment from a customer and send money to a supplier without visiting a branch. Benefits include speed and reach. Risks include fraud, failed transactions and dependence on agent cash and network coverage.

sections.heading: Core and open banking
sections.text: A core banking system is the central software that records customer accounts, balances and transactions and connects branches, cash machines and phone apps. Open banking lets customers, with consent, share their account data with licensed third parties through application programming interfaces (APIs). This can support budgeting apps or faster loans. Rules differ: the United Kingdom and the European Union have formal open banking regimes, Nigeria has issued its own guidelines, and many countries are still developing theirs. Security and consent are central.

sections.heading: Blockchain and robo-advisory
sections.text: A blockchain is a distributed ledger that records transactions in linked blocks across many computers. Cryptoassets are digital assets that use cryptography and distributed ledgers; their prices are volatile and rules vary widely by country. Robo-advisory uses online questionnaires and algorithms to suggest or manage investments, usually at low cost. It suits simple goals but may lack human judgement for complex needs.

sections.heading: Benefits, risks and rules
sections.text: Fintech can lower costs, widen access and speed service. It also brings fraud, cyberattack, outage, data privacy and money laundering risks. Regulation therefore covers licensing, payment systems, data protection and anti-money laundering. Financial inclusion improves when people can save and transact safely, but digital literacy, connectivity, fees and agent liquidity can exclude others. Adoption and rules vary by country, so check the current central bank and data protection authority guidance.

keyPoints: Digital payments move money electronically; mobile money links stored value to a phone and agent network.
Core banking systems record accounts and transactions across branches and channels.
Open banking shares account data through APIs with customer consent and licensed providers.
Blockchain is a distributed ledger; cryptoassets use it but remain volatile and unevenly regulated.
Robo-advisory gives automated investment advice from algorithms and questionnaires.
Fintech aids inclusion but needs regulation for fraud, privacy, cyber risk and money laundering; rules vary by country.

en.title: Development Finance and Microfinance
en.short: Microfinance models, SME and rural finance, development banks, inclusion, impact and sustainability.

sections.heading: What development finance does
sections.text: Development finance is finance for projects whose social returns are real but not fully captured by private lenders, so it often comes with long maturities, guarantees or subsidies. Development banks, national or multilateral, provide wholesale funds, long-term loans and technical help. Microfinance supplies small loans, savings, insurance and payments to low-income households and microenterprises. Financial inclusion means access to useful and affordable services, not merely opening an account; usage and quality matter too.

sections.heading: Microfinance models
sections.text: Group lending, made famous by Grameen Bank in Bangladesh, lends to small groups whose members guarantee one another, reducing screening and enforcement costs where collateral is scarce. Individual lending suits larger borrowers with records. Village banks are member-owned savings and credit groups. Savings-led models build deposits first. SME finance uses working capital, leasing, trade finance and credit guarantees. Rural finance must handle seasonal cash flows, weather risk, weak collateral and long distances, often through cooperatives or value chains.

sections.heading: Impact and subsidy
sections.text: Impact assessment asks whether clients are better off than they would have been without the service. Good studies compare a treatment group with a counterfactual, using randomised trials or matching, and measure income, business growth and empowerment. Selection bias and spillovers can mislead. Subsidies can support outreach, but they must be transparent and time-bound. Sustainability means covering costs from revenue. Example: 1,000 one-year loans average US$500, interest 30% a year, revenue US$150,000. Costs: administration US$120,000, funding US$25,000, loan losses 5% of US$500,000 = US$25,000. Total US$170,000. Deficit US$20,000, so subsidy or lower costs are needed.

sections.heading: Over-indebtedness risks
sections.text: Over-indebtedness means a borrower cannot meet repayments without harming basic living. It grows when several lenders lend to the same client, credit information is weak, collection is aggressive and borrowers are pressured to repay from new loans. Risks include default, distress and loss of trust. Consumer protection, credit bureaus, transparent pricing and responsible lending help. Microfinance should aim at both outreach and sustainable institutions.

keyPoints: Development finance targets social returns that private lenders may not capture.
Microfinance models include group lending, individual lending, village banks and savings-led groups.
SME and rural finance need products that fit working capital, seasonality and weak collateral.
Impact assessment compares outcomes with a credible counterfactual, not just before-and-after figures.
Revenue = number of loans × average loan size × interest rate; sustainability needs revenue to cover administration, funding and loan losses.
Over-indebtedness can be reduced by credit information, responsible lending and consumer protection.

en.title: Research Methods in Finance
en.short: Designing finance research, collecting sound data, testing hypotheses and writing up.

sections.heading: Design and review
sections.text: Research design is the plan linking question, evidence and method. A finance question may be descriptive, explanatory or predictive. A literature review summarises what is known, identifies gaps and shows how your study adds. Use primary data you collect or secondary data already published, such as annual reports, central bank statistics or market prices. Check definitions and units before comparing sources.

sections.heading: Data and sampling
sections.text: Sampling means choosing a subset of a population. In finance, samples are often all listed banks or firms meeting criteria, called purposive or census sampling, not random. State inclusion rules and period. Data quality covers accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness. Clean data: match dates, remove duplicates, check outliers and document changes. Missing values must be reported, not hidden.

sections.heading: Hypothesis and regression
sections.text: A hypothesis is a testable statement about a relationship, for example the null hypothesis, H0: bank size has no effect on profitability. Basic regression estimates y = a + bx + e, where y is the dependent variable, x the independent variable, a the intercept, b the slope and e the error. Example with made-up units: y = 8, 10, 12 and x = 1, 2, 3. Mean x = 2, mean y = 10. b = Σ[(x − 2)(y − 10)] ÷ Σ(x − 2)² = (2 + 0 + 2) ÷ (1 + 0 + 1) = 4 ÷ 2 = 2. a = 10 − 2 × 2 = 6. So y = 6 + 2x. Check: x = 3 gives 12. A low p-value means the result is unlikely if H0 is true, but it does not prove causation.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Research ethics require honesty, informed consent, confidentiality and no fabrication or plagiarism. Cite every source. A dissertation usually has title, abstract, introduction, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Present tables clearly, label units, and explain what each result means. Keep a data file and code so another person can check your work.

keyPoints: Research design links the question, data and method before collection starts.
Secondary data must be checked for definition, unit, period and quality.
State sampling rules and report missing values.
Simple regression is y = a + bx + e, with b = Σ[(x − mean x)(y − mean y)] ÷ Σ(x − mean x)² and a = mean y − b × mean x.
A low p-value means the result is unlikely if the null hypothesis is true, but it does not prove causation.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, accurate citation and no fabrication or plagiarism.

en.title: Advanced Banking Theory
en.short: Why banks intermediate, how information and liquidity problems cause runs, and why regulation is debated.

sections.heading: Intermediation theories
sections.text: Financial intermediation channels funds from savers to borrowers. Transaction-cost theory says pooling achieves economies of scale. Information-production theory says banks screen and monitor borrowers, reducing duplicated effort. Delegated-monitoring theory (Diamond, 1984) says depositors appoint a bank to monitor, but the bank must itself be monitored. Liquidity-insurance theory (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983) says banks offer demand deposits against illiquid loans. Limits: technology lowers costs, monitoring incentives are imperfect, and liquidity insurance creates fragility.

sections.heading: Information asymmetry
sections.text: Information asymmetry means one party knows more than the other. Before contracting, adverse selection arises: risky borrowers are more eager to seek funds, so lenders may ration credit instead of raising rates (Stiglitz and Weiss). After contracting, moral hazard arises: borrowers may take more risk because lenders bear part of any loss. Banks use screening, collateral, covenants and monitoring. Limits: collateral excludes asset-poor borrowers, screening is costly, and relationship lending can lock borrowers in.

sections.heading: Liquidity and runs
sections.text: Liquidity transformation means funding long-term, illiquid assets with short-term, liquid liabilities. It gives savers ready cash and firms long-term finance, but creates maturity mismatch. A bank run is a self-fulfilling panic: if depositors expect others to withdraw, each rushes to be first. Diamond and Dybvig show deposit insurance or a lender of last resort can stop panic, but both create moral hazard. Limits: runs also hit non-banks and wholesale funding, and some reflect real losses.

sections.heading: Regulation and limits
sections.text: Regulation addresses market failures: systemic externalities from runs and asset sales, information gaps, monopoly power and consumer protection. Deposit insurance protects small savers but weakens market discipline; capital rules make banks absorb losses and liquidity rules help them meet withdrawals without selling assets in a panic. Limits: rules differ by country, can be gamed, and impose compliance costs; regulatory capture, where regulators come to serve the banks they oversee, is a risk. Theory gives competing predictions, so no single model settles policy. A case: a bank with 100 in cash and 100 in sound but illiquid loans owes 200 in deposits. If 150 depositors withdraw, it cannot pay without a quick asset sale or central bank help.

keyPoints: Financial intermediation theories explain banks through transaction costs, information production, delegated monitoring and liquidity insurance.
Information asymmetry creates adverse selection before lending and moral hazard after lending.
