Liquidity transformation funds illiquid assets with liquid liabilities, creating maturity mismatch and run risk.
Diamond and Dybvig show runs can be self-fulfilling and that deposit insurance or a lender of last resort can stop panic but create moral hazard.
Regulation is justified by systemic externalities, information gaps and consumer protection, but rules differ by country and can be gamed.
No single theory fully explains banking, so policy should weigh competing models and local evidence.

en.title: Financial Econometrics
en.short: Regression, time series, panel data, volatility models and event studies, with diagnostics and software interpretation.

sections.heading: Regression with financial data
sections.text: Ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates a linear model y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + ε. Financial returns are often skewed, volatile and correlated over time, so check linearity, residual autocorrelation, heteroskedasticity (non-constant error variance) and outliers. Use robust standard errors when the error variance is not constant, and clustered standard errors when errors correlate within firms or over time. Report coefficients with standard errors and explain economic size, not only significance. In R, Stata, EViews or Python, inspect residual plots and tests such as Breusch-Godfrey and White.

sections.heading: Time series and panels
sections.text: Many financial series are non-stationary: mean and variance change over time. Test with augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF); difference if needed. ARIMA models combine autoregressive (AR) and moving-average (MA) terms. Use information criteria and residual checks to choose orders. Panel data track several firms over time. Fixed-effects models control for unobserved firm traits; random effects assume those traits are uncorrelated with regressors. The Hausman test helps choose. Cluster standard errors by firm or time.

sections.heading: Volatility and events
sections.text: Volatility clusters: large shocks follow large shocks. ARCH and GARCH models estimate conditional variance. GARCH(1,1): σ²t = ω + α ε²t−1 + β σ²t−1. Persistence is α + β; near one means shocks fade slowly. Event studies measure abnormal returns around announcements. Estimate a market model over a clean estimation window, then compute abnormal return ARt = Rt − (α + βRm,t) and cumulative abnormal return (CAR) over the event window. Test CAR for significance.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Suppose a stock’s estimated market model is α = 0.001 and β = 1.2. On an event day the market return is 1.0% and the stock return is 2.5%. Expected return = 0.001 + 1.2 × 0.01 = 0.013, or 1.3%. Abnormal return = 0.025 − 0.013 = 0.012, or 1.2%. If the next day’s abnormal return is −0.004, the two-day CAR = 0.012 − 0.004 = 0.008, or 0.8%. A t-test compares this CAR with its standard error; software reports the estimate, standard error and p-value.

keyPoints: OLS fits y = β0 + β1x1 + ... + ε; financial errors often need robust or clustered standard errors.
Test stationarity with the augmented Dickey-Fuller test and difference non-stationary series before ARIMA modelling.
Panel fixed effects control for unobserved firm traits; the Hausman test compares fixed and random effects.
GARCH(1,1) models conditional variance as σ²t = ω + αε²t−1 + βσ²t−1, with persistence α + β.
An event study abnormal return is ARt = Rt − (α + βRm,t), and CAR sums AR over the event window.
Always report specification, diagnostics and economic interpretation, not only p-values.

en.title: Advanced Risk Management
en.short: Credit, market and operational risk models, VaR, expected shortfall, stress testing and model risk.

sections.heading: Risk measures
sections.text: Value at Risk (VaR) is the loss that will not be exceeded with a stated probability over a stated horizon. Expected shortfall (ES) is the average loss in the worst cases beyond VaR. VaR ignores the size of tail losses; ES uses them, so ES is coherent, meaning it satisfies the standard axioms for risk measures, but ES is harder to backtest. Both depend on assumptions: the horizon, the confidence level, the loss distribution and stable parameters. A 99% one-day VaR of 2,000,000 means a 1% chance of losing more than 2,000,000 in one day, not a maximum loss.

sections.heading: Credit and operational models
sections.text: Credit risk models estimate expected loss as PD × LGD × EAD, where PD is probability of default, LGD is loss given default and EAD is exposure at default. Unexpected loss needs a distribution, often from credit ratings or structural models such as Merton’s. Market risk models use volatility, correlations and historical or simulated price changes. Operational risk models combine internal loss data, scenarios and controls; simple regulatory approaches use size indicators such as gross income, in total or by business line. All models are approximations and carry model risk: wrong data, wrong form or misuse.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A portfolio has 1,000,000 exposure. PD is 2%, LGD is 40%. Expected loss = 0.02 × 0.40 × 1,000,000 = 8,000. If one-year 99% VaR is 50,000 and the average loss beyond it is 70,000, ES is 70,000. Check: expected loss is not VaR; it is the long-run average credit loss.

sections.heading: Backtesting and capital
sections.text: Backtesting compares predicted losses with actual outcomes. For VaR, count exceptions: too many breaches suggests underestimation; too few may mean an over-cautious model. Stress testing applies severe but plausible scenarios, such as a currency crash or default wave, because models calibrated on calm data fail in crises. Capital allocation assigns capital to business units by risk contribution, not just stand-alone risk. Regulators set capital rules; under Basel III banks hold capital against credit, market and operational risk, but local rules differ.

keyPoints: VaR is a quantile of the loss distribution; ES is the average loss beyond VaR.
Expected credit loss = PD × LGD × EAD.
VaR and ES depend on horizon, confidence level and distribution assumptions.
Backtesting counts exceptions; stress testing uses severe scenarios.
Model risk arises from bad data, wrong assumptions and misuse.
Capital allocation should reflect risk contribution and regulatory rules, which differ by country.

en.title: Advanced bank regulation and financial stability
en.short: Systemic risk, macroprudential tools, resolution, fintech rules and national differences.

sections.heading: Systemic risk and macroprudential policy
sections.text: Systemic risk is the danger that a shock to one bank or market spreads through the financial system and disrupts credit and payments for the wider economy. It grows with size, interconnectedness and common exposures. Macroprudential policy uses rules aimed at the whole system, not one bank. Examples are a countercyclical capital buffer, which asks banks to hold more capital in booms, and limits on loan-to-value ratios in mortgages. These tools aim to lean against credit bubbles and build buffers before stress arrives. They sit beside microprudential supervision, which checks individual institutions.

sections.heading: Crisis management and resolution
sections.text: Crisis management covers central bank liquidity support, government guarantees and coordinated action when confidence falls. Resolution is the orderly restructuring or wind-down of a failing bank so that critical functions continue. Modern regimes prefer bail-in, where shareholders and some creditors absorb losses, over bail-out with public money. Deposit insurance protects small depositors, and a bridge bank can take over good assets. A made-up case: Kano Trust Bank suffers a run. The regulator uses a bridge bank, writes down shareholders, converts some bonds to equity and transfers insured deposits. This keeps payments running without a taxpayer rescue.

sections.heading: Comparative regulation and fintech
sections.text: Basel Committee standards are not law. Countries implement them differently: the United States has several federal and state regulators; the European Union runs a banking union in which the European Central Bank supervises large banks; Nigeria’s central bank supervises banks, and the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation insures deposits. Fintech adds pressure. Payment firms, electronic money issuers and crypto assets may fall outside bank rules. Regulators use sandboxes, such as the UK Financial Conduct Authority sandbox, to test innovations under limits. The balance is hard: tight rules can slow competition and new services, while light rules can allow instability. National choices reflect legal traditions, market size and political priorities.

keyPoints: Systemic risk arises when shocks spread through interconnected banks and markets.
Macroprudential policy uses system-wide tools such as countercyclical capital buffers and loan-to-value caps.
Resolution aims to wind down a failing bank without taxpayer bail-out, often through bail-in.
Deposit insurance and bridge banks help protect depositors and critical functions.
Basel standards are implemented differently in each country.
Fintech sandboxes test innovation but must be balanced against stability.
